analysis.one_liner: Triples the maximum fines companies face for workplace safety violations and adjusts them for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Labor Committee for nearly two years and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have roughly tripled the civil fines that employers can be charged under the Occupational Safety and Health Act — raising the top penalty from $10,000 to $30,000 and most other penalties from $1,000 to $3,000 [S3]. It also would have required the Labor Department to raise those fine amounts every five years to keep pace with inflation, so the penalties would not quietly shrink in value over time [S3]. Stronger fines give companies a bigger financial reason to fix unsafe conditions before workers get hurt. The bill was referred to the Senate Labor Committee, got a subcommittee hearing, and was never reported out.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hazardous jobs. Higher fines make safety violations more expensive, which gives employers stronger reason to guard machines, limit toxic exposures, and fix hazards before an inspection finds them. An inflation adjustment would have kept those penalties meaningful for decades instead of letting them erode.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum penalty for the most serious OSHA violations from $10,000 to $30,000 per violation [S3].
Raises most other OSHA civil penalties from $1,000 to $3,000 per violation [S3].
Requires the Secretary of Labor to adjust the maximum fines for inflation every five years using the Consumer Price Index, so penalty amounts do not lose value over time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who violate workplace safety rules, chiefly in industries like manufacturing, construction, and meatpacking where OSHA citations are common. Companies that already comply would pay nothing; the cost falls on those cited for violations.

drawbacks.text: The penalties would fall hardest on smaller employers, since the bill sets the same dollar limits for a large corporation and a small shop; a $30,000 maximum per violation is a much heavier burden for a small firm [S3].

Bigger fines alone do not make workplaces safer if inspections stay rare — a penalty only deters a company that expects to get caught, so enforcement staffing matters as much as the fine amounts [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is modest and well-targeted: the fines being tripled are maximum penalties for actual violations, not new costs on compliant employers. The inflation adjustment fixes a real problem — OSHA penalty caps had stayed flat while their deterrent value eroded. The main honest objection is that small businesses face the same dollar exposure as large ones, and that fines work only when inspections back them up.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Labor Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and died when the Congress ended without the committee ever sending it to the floor.

narrative.text: Senator Lautenberg introduced the bill on March 1, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
On March 9, 1989, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Labor, and the committee asked the Labor Department and the Office of Management and Budget for their comments [S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on May 1, 1990, but the full committee never reported the bill, and no floor vote ever happened before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced tripled fines for safety violations are better off, since the stronger penalties never became law and OSHA's fine levels stayed at their old amounts.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to triple OSHA civil penalties and index them to inflation; it was his lone sponsorship, with no cosponsors.

for.name: Subcommittee on Labor
for.role: Senate Labor and Human Resources Subcommittee on Labor
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on May 1, 1990, the furthest step the bill reached.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 1, 1989 and never reported it out; after a subcommittee hearing in May 1990, no markup or committee vote followed, and the bill died there.

against.name: Office of Management and Budget
against.what_they_did: Was asked by the committee for its comments on the bill in March 1989; the record shows no result from that request before the bill stalled.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no recorded opposition — the bill died quietly in committee with a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Employers subject to OSHA regulation (manufacturing, construction, and other hazardous industries)
industries.note: The bill would have tripled the maximum civil fines for safety violations and raised them with inflation, making violations more expensive. Those fines exist to push companies to fix hazards that injure workers, so the industry's interest in lower penalties runs against worker safety.
